on the boiler deck directly over the boilers þÿ reported One of the firemen, who was saved, says he had occasion to go on the deck, and seeing the demijohns, removed them They were replaced, but by whom is not known )m mediately previous to the bursting forth of j the flames, as several on hoard have assured us. a slight explosion was heard The demi johns had probably burst with the lv at. and their inflammable contents, taking fire instant ly, communicated to every part ol the boat, which having been freshly varnished caught as if it had been gunpowder. The heart bleeds at the thought. It is a singular coincidence that the Erie was burned at almost identically the same spot where the Washington was burned in June, 1838. Buffalo, Aug 10, 1841 The following is from Mr I'armelee, the bar keeper of the boat þÿ Perfect confusion succeeded, in the midst of which the small boat, hanging astern, was lowered by the hands and brought to the side. After a few

ladies had been handed down, the Irerizv ol those behind became uncontrolahle, and numbers leaped in beyond the capacity of the boat to sustain tin in, and it swamped. Several of those who fell from the boat were drawn under the wheel, and there were

jcxs drowned; while a few clung to the boat's sides and were finally saved A second and third boat were rendered useless bv the same infatuation Some five minutes after tin' appearance of the fire the machinery became deranged and stopped. Twenty minutes only bad elapsed from (lie beginning of the fire, after the intenseness of the heat had forced overboard every other person, when Captain Titus threw himself into the water and abandoned the boat to its fate. The few who then remained alive were tossirg in the midst of a heavy swell dependent upon the piecurious support, one, of an oar, another of a plank or box, and liable every tn ment to lose their hold through exhaustion and the benumbing efleets of fright. The steamboat I ady returned with the two she bad picked up to Dunkirk ; one of them was my informant He had thrown himself oveiboard on a plank, when he saw farther eflorts to he useless, but relinquished it to a friend who could not swim, and took for his own support the "fender," which just then fell by his side, lie states that those who survived the swamping of the boat, clung with desperation to the burning wreck, except as a t« w found other support. The first and main feature in this domestic condition is the depression of trade, which unfortunately has become so palpable as to admit of no denial This subject is well and fully stated in a passage of the Manchester Courier, of which the following is an extract : þÿ " We would fain he spared the pain of week alter week having to report continued embarrassments, losses, and unprofitable business in the commercial world; but duty and truth compel us to do so. A more harassing week in business than the past we do not recollect to have known. There has been a great want of confidence manifested, and when parties have been compelled to force sales, the most ruinous sacrifices have been made. Orders, whether for yarn cr goods, have been exceedingly restricted, considering the season of the year, and invariably executed at declining rates. To tell the number of spinning and manufacturing concerns which arc at a total stand, or only partially worked, and of the multitude of honest operatives thrown out of employment, and reduced to beggary and starvation, would be next too impossible, and appal the stoutest heart. Let any man lake a survey within a circle of 12 miles round Manchester, and see the dilapidated and deserted dwellings, the miserable and meagre wretches seeking about the country for work, or craving a morsel of bread; let him mark the signs of bankruptcy, and a ruinous depreciation of property, which everywhere meet him, and then ask himself if such a commercial hurricane ever devasled

the country before It is indued, unfortunate for the ensuing commencement of the conservative ministry, that wo i things should combine together, at the present time to cast a gloom over the country, the prospect of an unfavourable and laic harvest, and this undeniable depression m every branch of our manufactures I he failures in Lancashire, in Glasgow, and m Paisley , have indeed been very great and alarming of late ; they have not been visited by a m. re breeze, which has shaken off only a few leaves and broken away one or two superfluous branches ; their xisitaiion has been that of a sweeping storm which has levelled everything in i,s way> nn<| þÿ()r k n "!> houses and establishments which seemed to have been built for centuries This is much to he regretted, as it deprives the poorer classes of their usual employments, an I cl arks the progress of credit and accommodation upon which trade subsists.

THE VETO We give this anxiously looked "for document to day ; it was received about ten o'clock this morning. We invite every one of our renders to peruse it for himself Comments of ours are not called for to day. Ail we have to sav now is þÿ that there is nothing In it which should lead to a dissolution of tiie Cabinet, or destrov the integrity of the Whig party. We are indebted to the editors of the Sun for an early copy of the message. MESSAGE. OF THE PRKStOFNT OP THE UNITED STATES. RETrRMW WITH HIS OBJEC- TION'S, THE BILL TO INCORPORATE, THE FISCAL BANK OF THE U. STATES, AUGUST 16. 1841 To rur; Senate of the United States : The bill entitled ' An act to incorporate the subscribers to the Fiscal Bank of the United States." which originated in the Senate uaK fven considered by me, with a sino.ere desire 10 conform my action in regard to it. to that o' the two houses of Congress By the constitution it is made mv duty, either to approve the hill by signing it, or to return it with mv objections to the house in which it originated. I cannot conscientiously give- it mv approval, and I proceed to discharge the duty required of me by the constitution þÿ to give mv reasons for disapproving. The power of Congress to create a national bank to operate per se over the Union, has been a question of dispute from the origin of our government. Men most justly and deservedly esteemed for their high intellectual endowments, their virtue and their patriolismt have, in regard to it, entertained different

and conflicting opinions. Congresses have differed. The approval of one ('resident has been followed by the disapproval of another. Th ' people at different times have anquisbed in decisions both for and against, ( he country has been and still is deeply agitated bv this unfilled question. It will suffice for mc to say. that my own opinion has been uniformly proclaimed to be against the exercise of any such power by this government. On ail suitable occasions, during a period ol twenty five vears the opinions thus entertained have been unreservedly expressed 1 declared it in the Legislature of my native Stale. In the House of Representatives of the United States it has been openly vindicated by tne. In the Senate chamber, in the presence and hearing of many who are at this time members of that body, it has been affirmed and reaffirmed, in speeches and reports there made, and by votes there recorded. In popular assemblies I have unhesitatingly announced it; and in the last public declaration which I made, and that but a short time before the late Presidential election, I referred to my previously expressed opinions as being those then en'ertained by me : with a full knowledge of the opinions thus entertained! and never concealed, I was elected by the p"ople Vice President oi the United Stales. þÿ By the occurrence of a contingency provided for by the constitution, and arising under an impressive dispensation of Providence. I succeeded to the Presidential office. Before en-
tering Upon I ho duties of that ofTice, I took an oath that I would " preserve, protect and defend the coiisiiiutiun of tiio United States.'

Entertaining the opinions alluded to. and having taken this oath, the Senate and the country will see that I could not give my sanction to measure 8 of the character des eribed, withbut surrendering all claim to the respect of honorable men all confidence þÿ on the part of the people þÿ all self respect þÿ all regard for moral and religions obligations, without an observance of which no government can be prosperous, and no people can he bappv. It would bp lo commit a crime which 1 would not wilfully commit to gain any earthly reward, and which would justly subject me to the ridicule and scorn of all virtuous men. I deem it entirely unnecessary at this time to enter upon the reasons which have brought my mind to the convictions I feel and entertain on this subject. They have over and over again been repeated. If some oi ihose who have preceded me in this high office have entertained and avowed difteient opinions. 1 yield all confidence that their convic tions were sincere. I claim only to have the same measure meted out to myself. V\ uhout going laither into the argument. I will sav that, iu looking to ihe power of this Government to collect, safely keep, and disburse the public revenue, and incidentally regulate, commerce and exchange. Who shall minister to a mind deceased ; Pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow ; R ize out, the written troubles of the brain ; And cleanse the foul bosom of that perilous stuff Which weighs upon the heart? I open wounds over which Time tias no healing influence ; 1 open them as a warning to others þÿ an a beacon to show where manv a mortal's happiness is wrecked. The affliction of death is not an adequate punishment for the crime of murder: there is a misery far beyond this þÿ it is that of living þÿ living to feel the heinous consequences of guilt, to suffer the stinging of a restless conscience, and to have no refuge from its constant torments. My life has been a revolution of eventful vicissitudes, yet in the varied scenes of misery through which I have been doomed to pass, there has been one shade more dense than all the rest þÿ one tinge of moral hopelessness to which my other griefs are but idle imaginings, as trivial records. It is true, indeed, that the world looks upon me with an eye of complacency ; and that in

love, obedience, troops of friends but these empty vanities 1 turn from with a galled spirit, and envy the nothingness and oblivion which may not shroud the remnant of my miserable existence þÿ for 1 am a murderer I þÿ the murderer of helpless infancy ! ! þÿ This is the sorrow which has, like the Upas tree, poisoned every prospect, and has called forth from the oppressed brain withering thoughts that the word cannot know þÿ , My history is simple but could I record þÿ mv countless tears, the example would not pass away undeeded. My parents were in the middle station of life, and at an early age I was married to a person in a similar rank of society. We lived contented, and therefore happy. Our residence was in a large town in a western county, from whence my husband was accidentally called to transact some business, which detained him some months from home. He left me the mother of a healthy hoy ; he found me but the fearful word will come soon enough. To beguile the weary moments of my þÿhusband absence, s I was induced at intervals to mingle with society, and ttiis led me from my home. 1 had, perhaps, been allowed too much indulgence by mv parents, who accustomed me to continual gaieties, so that solitude came upon me as a feartul blank, as a melancholy. One dreadful night þÿ the memory of which will never lose its deep intensity þÿ 1 had undressed mv smiling boy, then about three years old ; he took his farewell of me after I had joined his tiny hands in prayer, and 1 then left him

to enjoy that peaceful repose which 1 hoped would renew his health and vigor. Happy are the affluent ! their tender nurslings are fostered by care, and shielded by studied attention. But this was not to be my blessed lot. nor that of my darling hov ; yet was he as beauteous as tfie richest and the proudest ol them ad, and his caresses to me were as dear as if he had tieen arrayed in the splendid robes of opulence, I was living in lodgings, and my only two apartments communicated by a door which generally remained þÿopen. ceived a shock in the calamity of his child When I left mv child that night, sleeping wilh bis face pillowed upon his downy arm, 1 had no intention of going beyond the next room, where 1 sat down, and imagination toon

brought to my mind the gaieties of my yo uh, and my loneliness became irksome. At this time a thoughtless companion called, and wishod me to accompany her to a card party. 1 went, the cheerfulness of the assemblage in duced me to prolong my absence, ami hours passed by unheeded. At length a returning sense of my duty called me home. I had relied upon the generally sound slumbers of mv child, and imagined I should find him asleep, as I had done when 1 had previously indulged in the fatal practice. 1 found the inmates of the house where 1 lodged in a state of confusion þÿ some horrid words caught my ear as 1 rustled along þÿ the door of my apartment was broken open, and my boy þÿ my rosy cherub þÿ lay there a blackened and disfigured sufferer. His pain was too intense tor the usual cries ol infancy, but in their stead he uttered a plaintive continued moan, every tone of which echoed the dying peal of my happiness, 1 wss frantic with grief, but my sorrow availed not. 1 watered his wounds with my tears. 1 would have given worlds þÿ I would have given every hope of joy to hear the slightest word ol endearment from his swollen lips, but he never spoke again I And in the moment when the last sigh of dissolving. and even now it glares upon me þÿ I must pause a few more tears have I shed to thy memory, my child ! 1 would lam complete my sorrowlul task, and not permit vain regrets to be the only truit of my penitence þÿ '1 he fearful tale ol my boy s accident was soon rudely told by the unfeeling witnesses of my agony. from the Jamaica Morning Journal Sept 24. 'LAUNCH OF THREE STEAM FRIGATES.

Within a few days of each other three of these splendid Steam Frigates have been launched into that element in which they are destined to perform the important functions of facilitating the communication between Great Britain and the Colonies. The first is the Thames, which was launched at Northfleet, on Thursday last, being the first of four large steamers in the course of building for the ' Royal Mail Steam Packet Company,'' by the Contractor, Mr. Pitcher. The ship is now at Black wall to receive her engines and fittings. We have yet to icatn her power. The sister ships .Medway, Iris, and Trent, building by the same enterprising contractor, are progressing. The Medway will be launched in about a month.

On Friday last, at noon, the steam frigate So! way was launched from the building yard of Mr. James M'Milan Greenock. The day being fine, a large concouise of people attended, and every spot from which the launch could be viewed was crowded with persons anxious to see this magnificent vessel descend into the water. On the signal being given she began to move, and glided down the ways in fine style. A correspondent describes this vessel as the largest steamer ever built in Scotland, measuring, asshe does 1,871 tons The Sol way is one of the fleet of frigates belonging to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. Which are intended to carry the West India Mails in time of peace, and in case of a war to act against the enemy. The fleet, as weforrnerly stated, when noticing the launch of the Cl\ de and T weed is to consis! of foiirieen ; but we understand that ten ol these difler from the other tour, and that the Sol way is the first of her kind that has yet been launched. She is built altogether of British and African oak, and with diagonal iron and wooden fastenings from stem to steru, as is done in her Majesty's steam fiigates We may add that her engines are the workmanship of Messrs. Scott, Sinclair & Co. þÿ 'Greenock Advertiser.'

CHINA, INDIA, AND EGYPT. Bv an express from Marseilles, in anticipation of the overland mail from India, we have received letters from China, India, and the shores of the Mediterranean, as well as files of all the newspapers published in the British possessions throughout the East. The latest dates are þÿ from Canton Hay 19, Macao May 20. Calcutta July 5, Bombay July 19, Alexandria August 20 and Malta August 26. The news from China, which comes down to the 20ih May, is the great matter of interest which we have received by this mail. þÿ The accounts from Canton describe the Chinese mandarins as most decidedly hostile to the British, and state that the truce allowed to Captain Elliot, during which a large export Of tea had been effected, had in reality no other object than to enable them to lake measures for expelling t he barbarians. The emperor continues to fulminate proclamations, not only against the invaders of his country, hut also against such of the mandarins and officers as he conceives do not do their duty most efficiently A large army was collecting in the . neighbourhood of Canton, which city was> notwithstanding its great trade, deserted by numbers of the inhabitants, who appear to dread their own soldiery as much as they do the foreigners. Captain Elliot, whose great object appears hitherto to have been to secure the annual export of tea, was still temporising with the Chinese authorities, and had succeeded in having 11,000,600 lb. shipped before the 18th of May ; and there were hopes that an equal

or greater quantity would he on board before the enu of that month. Hong Kong was again Occupied by the British, and the chief commissioner busied himself during some time in laving out plans for a city ; but on the 18ih ol May, at the time when it was said he and several ships were about to proceed anew to 1. rhelce, and there to demand a settlement ft on. the very court of Pekin, lit: went in the steamer Nemesis up to the Canton river, as if apprehensions were entertained of an attack bv the Chinese on the foreign factories, or on the Algerien and Modeste, stationed near them. It is therefore feared that ere this a conflict has occurred, in which the city of Canton may have been subjected toar.onflagi <tion, in order to give the Chinese a lasting example.

".VW' -.' In the mean time the preparations for carrying on the warfare with the Chinese continue in India. The new plenipotentiary, Sir Henry Pottinger and the admiral. Sir William Barker, arrived at Bombay ori the morning of tb<: 7 b of July, and set out for their ultimate destination on the 17th, in the steam frigate Sesosiris. '1 ho admiral examined the arsenal and dockyard of Bombay, to order to know their capabilities, for, as he said, " the Chinese dispute may be settled in a few months, or it may last for years." It is understood that the policy to be pursued bv 8ir Henry Bottinger, the now Plenipotentiary, and admiral Sir W. Barker, the Commandant ol the forces, is, as neatly as possible, the reverse of that which has been hitherto acted upon, and w ith such s goal ill success. A strict blockade of the whole ol the southern and western coast is immediately to be put in force ; the mouth of the great river is to he effectually guarded, and the utmost care is to be taken to avoid unnecessarily irritating the natives, who, from the first, have appeared to he favourably disposed. The island of Anioy will, it is said, he occupied, as soon as the dispositions for the blockade are completed ; and from its position, deeply embayed in the mainland, and nearly opposite to the island of Formosa, it is expected that it will be an excellent exchange for the pestilential Chilian. The monsoon, which has been attended with an unusual fall of rain, continued to paralyse all movements on this Bombay
side of India. The Bombay army west of the Indus has suffered much from sickness, particularly at Cotra. þÿ Unci Sept. 6.

All the offices of the administration are bow tilled, and it will be seen by the correct and complete list, which is given in our paper of this day, tliHt Sir 11. Peel has fully succeeded in the pledge and promise which he held forth to the people þÿ that in reforming her Majesty's household he would consult as much as possible, the royal feelings, and would confine its changes to those persons only, whom from an obvious point of prudence, it was absolutely necessary to remove from all contact and interference in politics with which it was improbable they could feel any sympathy. The ladies most conspicuously attadied to her þÿMajesty court s by the late ministry, have been succeeded by the Duchess of þÿBuccl uchand the Marchioness of Camden; a few other ladies of her Majesty's household being continued in their former situations, and particidarlv three of them, Lady Barham, Lady Portman, and Lady Lyttelton; we believe we may say all of them personally in great favour with her Majesty. The Duchess of Sutherland, in a domestic point of view, was undoubtedly, a great loss: þÿ a woman of the greatest personal beauty and elegance in the kingdom, and against whom even party iisell has never breathed a word. It is well observed by an excellent cotem- -porary þÿ that if it be true that her Majesty, in acting faithfully upon the principles of the constitution, has sacrificed some personal predilections, the readiness and frankness with which her Majesty lias made these sacrifices

will not be lost upon the nation, nor upon the party which, under her royal permission, now holds the reins of government. It is lor mean minds to cherish resentment against what may be supposed to be an unwilling compliance with circumstances. No such feeling exists in the breast of any true conservative. The party has sense enough and principle enough to view the reality of things through the medium of duty Jf they believe that her Maþÿjesty s personal preference was not towards them, they are not the less þÿ but the more sensible of the devotedness with which they ought to serve a Sovereign, who not only complies at once with the principles of the constitution, but does so even against the bias of her personal inclination þÿ who makes a sacrifice of her own liking in order to discharge the duties imposed upon her by her high position as constitutional Queen of a free people. As to the assertion of the whig journals I Ladies of the Bedchamber þÿ that the people are against the party now in power, we can make nothing of it by any process of reasonable examination. It seems to be the mere raving of failure and disappointment. The Whigs who constructed the Reform Act must condemn themselves if they say that the House of Commons, as at present constituted, does not represent the peo- j pie, and they are well aware that tiie voice of the House of Commons is certainly not with j them þÿ but more of this presently In order to reseat the new ministers in par- ! liamtnt, no less than twenty seven new wilts j

jtiobody, for it is well known that political ambition does not disturb bis mind. Gifted with the most inotterisive character in Gieat Britain. Lord Melbourne is goners lit liked by both parties, and this will be still more the case when he shall be no longer minister. þÿ He is now 63 years of age, and the native good nature of his mind is imprinted on his face. He will now have all the enjoyments of the court with iut the responsibility of government ; not indeed that he bore any considerable share of it , for the cabinet of Lord Melbourne might with more propriety have been called that of Lord John Itussell, who was its presiding genius. As to Lord Melbourne, he had always an air of astonishment whenaskeda question as Prime Minister, iu the House of Lords, and invariably replied, þÿ 1 really þÿdon know, t but 1 will þÿinquire. His last speech on the address was very characteristic. China and the Tea Trade. Our memory does not serve us at this moment as to the question, whether the British commissioner at Canton has in any way> direct or indirect, an interest in the trade in tea ; hut of this we are confident, that 10 out of 20 of the þÿ buyers" for the London tea houses would have shown, if placed in Captain Elliot's situation, a mind far less riveted to the attatrs of þÿ the þÿshop than has this representative of the British government. A leading error, firmly fixed in the Chinese mind from the first, has evidently been a persuasion that England was absolutely dependent on þÿ the Celestial þÿEmpire; and that, somehow or other, a supply of tea was positively essential to our very existence. And :f the British commissioner had desired to fix this impression still more firmly on the belief of that government, he could not have taken a course more calculated to do so than some of his latest movements. The more serious grew the prospects of the war þÿ the more furious the imperial þÿwrath the more fixed the resolve to þÿ exterminate the þÿforeigners the 1 more frantic appeared Captain þÿElliot s anxiety to buy tea ! The real character of the struggle does not seem ever to have been at all understood by him. The concerns of the tea market, then, must be put aside for a time. The Chinese must be made to understand that þÿ tea is not the first and last thing in tire view of the British government. So long as i lie þÿ opening or shutting of the þÿtrade is made the greatest of all questions, so long

will they misconceive both our position and their own. There is now, unhappily, but slilit apparent chance of terminating this aflair without the infliction of some fearful specimen o| ihe horrors of war. The protraction of the quarrel Iras increased the necessity lor some such calamity, and the longer it is delayed, the more severe, apparently will it require to be. Thus is it ever with weak and vacillating minds. They are sure to arrive at the very opposite point to that which they appear to he reaching. Captain Elliot has boon trying to carry on a þÿ little þÿwar a slight, and trivial, and half-in-earn-

We repeat our conviction that in all probability these remarks are hardly called for, inasmuch as all parties concerned are growing fully sensible of the fatuity of the course heretofore pursued.

The intelligence from China, of the capture and subsequent release of Canton, reached London on the 7th ot October; the advices received there being of precisely the same date that reached New York by ihe Narra gunsett. The papers are excessively severe on Captain Elliott for giving up the city, and some of them speak out very plainly on the moral aspecis of the case. The British forces had obtained a brilliant victory, but it bad a strange sequel. We last left Captain Elliot ' negotiating." þÿ The Chinese, as they bad 'done during previous liegociations, had employed the time so easily granted bv Captain Elliot, in strengthening their means of defence and attack. þÿ At length the Plenipotentiary seemed to have become aware of the lact. and he consented to a renewal of hostilities. The British troops were concentrated on Cantor: ; þÿ commanding points on the wails of the town were seized; the Chinese were unyielding; Sir þÿ Hugh Gough was just about to give the order for the tiual and complete conquest of the city, when þÿ Captain Eliiot was negotiating again I He consented to relinquish the conquest, and witlidiavv the British troops, upon condition that the Chinese army retire to a distance of sixty miles, arid that six millions ol dollars were paid He turned the victory gained by other officers, to a means of plundering the Chinese in the name ol the Queen of England. It is not clear in what light the payment is considered ; the English call the money " ransom" for the city ; but the Chinese call it "opium compensation"; and Captain Elliot appears to have applied it to pay " Dent &l Co," and "opium scrip" at Calcutta, if this is true, it looks as if he had committed an act of criminal insubordination ; lor the Brush Government, in disallowing Ins bills, had refused

to sanction bis bargain with the opium smugglers ; yet be seizes money obtained in the name ol his Government, and appropriates it to the payment of his personal liabilities, in defiance ol their express disallowance. This proceeding requires, however, to he more clearly explained The one thing is plain, that Captain Eliiot has converted a victoiy, which, so lar as Canton was concerned, might have been a decisive blow, into a plundering expedition on account ol the opium merchants ; he has interposed a new obstacle to the settlement ol Lord Palmersloe's "little war" þÿ now becoming a great one, or at least charged with very gigantic consequences ; he has hxed an indelible stain on the cause, already equivocal. The long-talked of insurrection in favor of Queen Christina broke out about the 1st of October, at Pampeluna. It was headed by General O'Donnell, who possessed himself of the citadel, having with him three battalions of foot, two squadrons of horse and a small body of artillery. The movement was quickly followed at Vittoiia and Bilboa, and indeed throughout Navarre and Guipuscoa it secmr to have been favored.

The plot extended to the capital, where on -attempt was made, to seize the person of the young Queen. but the insurrection there was put down almost in a moment bv Espartero, who was apprised of it beforehand and tully prepared to meet it. Diego Leon and General Concha, who were at the head ol the malcontents, escaped. A few days after some disturbances occurred at Barcelona, hut these seem to have been got up by a third party, adhering neither to Christina nor to Espartero. The latest accounts are to the 20th from Bayonne. O'Donnell had then marched from Pampeiuna and gained possession of Estelle. General Averbe was advancing to meet him, having tak n possession ol Pampeiuna alter its evacuation by U' Donnell At Madrid al' was quiet Diego Leon had been taken and shot. It was not doubted that the insurrection would finally he suppressed ; the provinces, but not until after a long term of ravages and bloodshed Queen Christina is reported to have officially disclaimed all connection with the plot, but her disclaimer was not believed- The King of the French aiso is charged with having some hand in it, as a preliminary to the marriage of iiis son, the Duke d'Auinale> with the young Queen Isabella. Concha and all the officers which were with him, finding their efforts hopeless, escaped by a private door into the country, and the soldiers, abandoned by their officers, laid down tfieii arms and surrendered at discretion. During the conflict the Queen and her sister are stated to have been in prayers, and calling for succour. Madame Mina was with them, and put mattresses near them to protect litem from the balls which entered the room. JV1. Gonzales, who was in the offices of the ministry, which are in the interior of the palace, bai> leaded himself, and the assailants endeavouied m vain to break open the doors- The troops who surrounded the palace and acted against the assailants, were caminanded by Espartero.
